content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a framework for mitigating bias focusing on intersectional bias. The framework reduces the mutual information between protected attributes at training time by incorporating a constant in the loss function. At test time, protected attributes are not necessary. The framework is evaluated on two unbalanced datasets and metrics are reported in terms of accuracy and standard fairness metrics. Reported results show that fairness metrics perform better than previous work without damaging accuracy.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The proposed method is simple and can be used for intersectional approaches as well as single-attribute approaches.
- The proposed method does not require protected attributes at test time, which are sometimes unavailable.
- The proposed method performs better than previous work in terms of fairness metrics without degrading accuracy.
- Several ablation studies by masking the protected attributes, correlated features, etc. are reported.

Weaknesses
- It is unclear which protected attributes are being evaluated in each dataset.
- In Figure 2, the unsampled method seems to work equally well as the proposed method. Can you discuss the benefits of not upsampling in more detail?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well-written and clear.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper addresses an important problem. Most methods for bias mitigation are focused on a single dimension, whereas intersectional bias can be hidden. The proposed solution looks simple and effective. The experiments are technically sound, and it seems that the proposed method outperforms previous work. Overall, this looks like solid work tackling an important problem.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper aims to mitigate intersectional subgroup bias by reducing the mutual information between protected attributes and the label attribute. To this end, the paper proposes a training algorithm with a fairness loss, where the fairness loss is used to approximately measure the mutual information between the attributes. Experiments are performed on the UCI Adult, Law School Admissions Council, and COMPAS datasets. The empirical results show several behaviors (e.g., sensitivity, baseline comparison) of the proposed algorithm.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]

S1: The paper tries to reduce the fairness gerrymandering problem by improving intersectional fairness, which is a very important issue in practice.

S2: The paper contains several interesting experiments. For example, Table 3 shows the sensitivity of the algorithms when masking the protected attributes, and Figure 3 describes the feature interaction effects of the biased and unbiased algorithms.

[Weakness]

W1: Although the paper aims to improve intersectional fairness, the proposed algorithm seems not specialized to solve the intersectional fairness issues, including the limited access to protected attributes and the scalability issues. It is unclear how the proposed algorithm is especially effective to those issues.

W2: The paper uses a proxy for measuring the mutual information between the protected and label attributes, but the the justification on the proxy is not enough. 
- One related work [1], which is cited in the paper, theoretically shows how the adversarial training framework can capture the mutual information between the protected attributes and the predicted labels. Several other works also provide theoretical discussions on fair training with mutual information [2]. 
- Compared to these works, this work’s proxy is not based on enough theoretical evidence. It would be much better if the paper can give clear discussion on how exact the proxy measure the mutual information.

[1] Cho et al., A fair classifier using mutual information, ISIT 2020
[2] Zhang et al., Mitigating unwanted biases with adversarial learning, AIES 2018

W3: Empirical results are not sufficient to demonstrate the advantages of the proposed algorithm. 
- For example, it seems the algorithm may not achieve high enough fairness in several scenarios. In Figure 1, the first and third graphs in the second row show that the proposed algorithm (blue) does not have high fairness points compared to other two methods. Also, the paper observes that the accuracy-fairness tradeoffs become similar with other methods in the high fairness regimes. However, we usually aim to achieve high fairness (say less than 0.1), then the proposed algorithm has no benefit in this practical scenario. 
- Moreover, in Figure 2, the proposed algorithm shows comparable fairness results (especially in DP cases) with upsampled baseline, which is very simple. Thus, it is quite questionable why we use the proposed method. 
- Relatively minor) Most experimental results are reported without the error ranges. 

W4: There is no detailed discussion on when the algorithm performs when equalized odds (EO) or demographic parity (DP). The paper argues that one benefit of their method is not targeting a specific fairness metric. However, simply debiasing the data may not enough high fairness in terms of EO and DP, thus it is unclear why only reducing the mutual information between the protected attribute and the true label (not predicted label) can be an attractive advantage in terms of group fairness. It would be better if the paper can clarify their method’s characteristics based on the previous insights in the literature, e.g., the impossibility theorem between EO and DP [1].

[1] Barocas et al., Fairness and machine learning, 2019
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I believe that the writing quality of the paper is reasonable. However, the paper may need to clarify the novelty of their work. Detailed comments are in the previous section.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although the paper focuses on an important model fairness issue and gives several interesting empirical results, there exist several limited aspects (W1–W4). Thus, I vote that this paper has room for improvement.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper presents a training algorithm that increases fairness measures (such as demographic parity and equalized odds) with respect to intersectional protected attributes with minimal effect on the overall accuracy of the model. In practice the method consists of adding a regularization term to the desired optimization objective. The regularization term seems to penalize predictions that give high probability to a randomly selected label when one feature (or one group of features) at the time is replaced by a baseline value. The method does not need to know a-priori which are the intersectional groups, instead all features (and combinations) are accounted for in the regularization term. 

Experiments are performed on tubular datasets such as LSAC, Adults and COMPAS (the latter only in the appendix) and against GerryFair (Kearns et al., 2018),  a mutual information-based approach (Cho et al., 2020) and a simple approach that upsamples underrepresented sub-groups. Results show that the method provides comparable accuracy at a similar or better equalized odd (computed as true positive rate difference and false positive rate difference) and demographic parity. Furthermore, results show that a model trained with the proposed regularization becomes robust to changes in the protected attributes in contrast to models where the protected attributes are simply removed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
- The empirical results show consistent improvements over the alternative algorithms used for the comparison.

Major weaknesses
- The explanation of the method lacks key details. Unfortunately such lack of explanation harms the clarity and the reproducibility of the method.
    - See Clarity section for more details.
- It in unclear to me if this model requires to know which are the protected attributes. The phrasing seems to imply that it dees not, but the results seem to tell a different story. For example, Table 4 shows that the model after being trained with the proposed regularization becomes “insensitive” to the protected intersectional features such as “race and gender”. The question is how does the model become insensitive ONLY to those protected features if all of them were equally perturbed during training? I think this needs to be explained better. Here are some potential explanations:
    - The model becomes insensitive ONLY to those protected attributes that are not correlated (this needs to be proven with ad-hoc experiments and it could be seen as a limitation since in some applications there is a correlation between protected attributes and prediction).
    - The model actually needs to know which are the protected attributes such that the regularization can be targeted to those attributes  only (in this case the phrasing in the paper would need to change).
- Since the method requires perturbations of attributes, its immediate application is limited to tabular data. 

Other comments
- I’d consider adding the reference and a discussion to “Minimax Pareto Fairness: A Multi Objective Perspective” from Martinez et al., since this method also does not require test-time access to sensitive attributes. Empirical comparison would also enrich the paper but I am aware that one cannot compare to everything. 
- I’d include in Table 3 also the upsampling strategy since it seems to be effective.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This is in my opinion the biggest weakness of this paper. As motioned above: too many details are missing in order for the method to be clear and reproducible. Here are some concrete examples:
    - In many instances the paper mentions a feature baseline x’ but it is unclear how this baseline is computed. For example:
        - “Let x′j ∈ Rd denote a shared baseline across all samples for input feature j.”
        - “We chose baseline values x′ carefully to indicate missingness of corresponding attributes in the dataset.” It is still unclear how was this chosen.
    - In equation 3 a function “f_c” is introduced but never defined. In the notation section a function “f” was introduced (the model that predicts a label) but it is unclear if here it means the same. What does the foot index C means? Is there a model per class?
    - In the experiments it is unclear what the set A is (is it all possible combinations of attributes or a smaller pre-defined set?). Note that A Is defined as “Let also A denote a set of the subsets of Ak” which I find a bit confusing.
    - The intuition behind equation 3 should be provided and discussed. Without the missing detail mentioned above (e.g, how does one define the set A or what is f_c?) I’d say that this term is penalizing predicting a random class (which when the number of classes is > 2 is often the “Wrong class”) with high confidence when some features are set to the baseline value. Is this correct? If so it should be explained, if not then the overall method is not clear.
    - After defining the method in equation (2) and (3) the experiments section says “As a bias mitigation constraint, LA , we used squared distance between the output and the provided label instead of cross entropy …” So Equation (2) is not what is actually being used for LA? I would explain this more clearly and provide the equation of what is actually being used.
    - “Table 2 shows how the mutual information between protected attributes Gender and Race reduces as we augment the data with samples that associate intersectional subgroups of protected attributes with random guesses. “ How was mutual information computed?
    - In the comparison with the up-sampling strategy how strong was the upsampling? I would try to help the reader to reproduce these results by providing all the needed details. Also could the upsampling strength be increased or was this tuned on a validation set to be the optimal (under some condition) upsampling strength? 
    - In the sub-section “Studying the effects of strongly correlated features with protected attributes” the paper reads “we use two race related features Race1 and Race” it is important to add which features those were. What is exactly Race1?
- Section 3.2 on information theory seems superfluous and contains potential mistakes. The paper tries to related the proposed method to information theory, specifically to mutual information. However, the method decreases the mutual information between input features and prediction by adding a regularization function but it does not analytically attempt to reduce mutual information. In practice:
    - I think that Equation (2) is not needed (Cleary conditioning on random labels increases the entropy of a variable)
    - “we propose a proxy measure of MI that can be incorporated into the optimization objective.” I don’t think that equation 3 can be called a proxy for Mutual Information. 
    - “The proxy measure aims to reduce the distance between S(xi,x′,Ak) and Unif(1,C)”. S() is a function that replace the value of some variable, while Unif() is a uniform sampling function. The two functions take different inputs and provide different outputs, it is unclear what reducing their distance means in this context.

Minor comment that could help further improve clarity 
- In order to make the paper self-standing instead of saying “We compute pairwise feature interactions based on the formulations in Tsang et al. (2020)” I would explain how the intersection is actually computed and add the citation.
- The results of  the “Feature interaction effects”  show that the interaction indeed changes but I am not sure what is the take home message.
- Avoid introducing notation if it is not used. For example “Analogously, x^{\A_k} denotes a subset of features that excludes protected attributes A_k”. I think this symbol is never used again in the paper. 
- Intersectional groups are defined in 3 ways (using the intersect symbol, using an underlined “and”, and using {.}). I would choose one way and be consistent throughout the paper.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper tackles an important problem: fairness of ML models. The results seem to support the effectiveness of the proposed regularization however the presentation of the method lacks too many details for a correct understanding and for the method to be reproducible. I’d encourage the authors to take the comments constructively in order to improve the clarity of their work and resubmit if this is rejected.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed to mitigate bias of protected attributes. The motivation is that previous works focus on mitigating one kind of bias, and this work aims to deal with bias of subgroup. To achieve this goal, this work proposed a fairness-aware learning algorithm based on mutual information. Experiments show that the proposed method outperforms baseline methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

\+ The motivation is clear. Instead of only mitigating the bias led by one protected attribute, this works further consider mitigating the bias led by any subgroup of protected attributes.

\+ The proposed method outperform baseline methods.

\+ The research problem is strongly related to fairness AI, which is an important problem in AI.

Weaknesses & Questions:

\- It is not clear to me why we need to focus on subgroup bias rather than single class bias. A straightforward solution is to deal with the single class bias separately rather than considering their intersection. Therefore, the importance of motivation is not clear. More detailed analysis on this (e.g., the analysis of subgroup bias and single class bias of data) may help.

\- The writing quality of this paper is not satisfying. This paper used several important terms without clear definition, e.g., fairness gap and intersectional bias, which makes it harder to understand the motivation and background. Please see below.

\- The term "fairness gap" is used many times in the paper, but there is no definition of this term. Could the authors explain more on fairness gap, fairness gerrymandering, and their importance?

\- Similarly, could the authors define "intersectional (subgroup) bias"?

\- The introduction section is not informative enough. For the method, this section introduced the motivation of reducing the mutual information between intersectional subgroups and the output variable. However, the details of the method to achieve this goal are not clear.

\- Table 1 shows the comparisons with three baseline models. However, it is not clear what the baseline models are, e.g., architecture or model name.

\- In Section 3.1, what does "shared baseline" mean?

\- In Section 4, the terms EO and DP are used without introduction or definition.

\- The method has an underlying assumption that the protect attributes are known in advance (according to Section 3.1). This is not a reason to reject the paper, but is the limitation of the method.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please see "Strengths and Weaknesses" for the detailed comments. Due to the missing details and explanations, I don't think it is easy to reproduce the results. Also, the clarity is not good.
content.summary_of_the_review:
My initial rating is actually between 3 and 5. Overall, I am leaning towards negative.

The strength is the straightforward motivation: instead of only mitigating the bias led by one protected attribute, this works further consider mitigating the bias led by any subgroup of protected attributes. It is easy to summarize the motivation.

The weaknesses are (1) why the motivation is important (more detailed and deeper analysis are needed), (2) the unclear definition of terms, (3) how the proposed differs from previous works (detailed comparisons are needed).

Considering the motivation and writing quality, I think this version is not ready for publication.
